displayQuote: A life spent making mistakes is not only more honorable, but more useful than a life spent doing nothing

meta.title: Who really said "A life spent making mistakes is not only more honorable, but more useful than a life spent doing nothing"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — George Bernard Shaw wrote it in his 1911 Preface on Doctors to The Doctor's Dilemma. The popular version quietly drops one word.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A life spent making mistakes is not only more honorable, but more useful than a life spent doing nothing'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Shaw — from his 1911 preface to The Doctor's Dilemma. Verified against the primary text, with the original 'in making mistakes' wording.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Shaw wrote this in the “Preface on Doctors” to his play The Doctor’s Dilemma, published by Brentano’s in 1911. It is confirmed verbatim in the full text of the preface ↗ — though Shaw’s original reads “a life spent in making mistakes.”

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Attention and activity lead to mistakes as well as to successes; but a life spent in making mistakes is not only more honorable but more useful than a life spent doing nothing. The one lesson that comes out of all our theorizing and experimenting is that there is only one really scientific progressive method; and that is the method of trial and error.
trail: Confirmed verbatim in the Project Gutenberg text of the preface ↗: “a life spent in making mistakes is not only more honorable but more useful than a life spent doing nothing.”
Quote Investigator ↗ traces it to the “Preface on Doctors,” Brentano’s 1911 edition, pp. lxxxv–lxxxvi.
The play The Doctor’s Dilemma premiered in London in 1906; the essay-length preface appeared with the 1911 Brentano’s edition (per Quote Investigator). The full play and preface are on Wikisource ↗.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular version drops the “in” and adds a comma
source.excerptNote: The sentence sits in Shaw’s argument that even a democracy’s clumsy meddling beats passive neglect — his case for trial and error as the only genuinely progressive method.

author.name: George Bernard Shaw
author.heading: About George Bernard Shaw
author.bio: George Bernard Shaw was an Irish playwright, critic and polemicist whose plays — among them Pygmalion, Man and Superman and Saint Joan — made him the most significant British dramatist since Shakespeare. He was awarded the 1925 Nobel Prize in Literature. His plays typically carry long, argumentative prefaces; the one to The Doctor’s Dilemma is a broadside against the medical profession in which this sentence appears.

misattribution.heading: Correctly credited — but usually misquoted
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Shaw is sound. What circulates online is a lightly altered wording, not a wrong author.

items.why: Popular quote sites render it without Shaw’s word “in” and add a comma after “honorable.” Shaw’s original text ↗ reads “a life spent in making mistakes is not only more honorable but more useful than a life spent doing nothing.”

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the words are genuinely Shaw’s, from his 1911 Preface on Doctors ↗ — just quote them with the “in.”

context.heading: Why he wrote it
lead: The sentence is not a standalone aphorism but a step in an argument. Shaw is defending public scrutiny of the medical profession, insisting that even a democracy’s clumsy interference is better than leaving doctors to police themselves.

“Attention and activity lead to mistakes as well as to successes,” he grants — but the alternative, doing nothing, is worse. From this he pivots to his real claim: that trial and error is “the only really scientific progressive method.”
context.pull: There is only one really scientific progressive method; and that is the method of trial and error.
